sections.body: The AI Economist covers the places where machine learning has moved from research papers into the daily work of forecasting, trading, lending and investing. In macroeconomics, models now blend traditional econometrics with text and high frequency data to nowcast output, inflation and employment between official releases. In trading, machine learning ranks signals, sizes positions and executes orders, while in credit it scores borrowers and flags early signs of distress. Private equity teams use it to screen targets and parse filings, and portfolio managers use it to estimate risk and rebalance. The common thread is not a robot that replaces judgement, it is software that reads more data, faster, than any analyst could.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this field are genuinely settled. Short horizon forecasting of liquid prices remains close to a random walk, and most published trading signals decay once costs and crowding are included. Credit scoring is mature and heavily regulated, so gains there come from better features and monitoring rather than new model classes. What is not solved is causal inference, regime change and the long tail of rare events, which is exactly where losses concentrate. Language models read filings and earnings calls well but still confabulate, so every output needs a human check. Governance is the least settled area, because nobody has agreed on how to audit a model that changes with its data.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader can start with Macroeconomic Econometrics for the forecasting base, then move to Quantitative Trading and Fixed Income and Credit Risk for the two largest applications of prediction to prices and default. Private Equity and Deal Sourcing and Portfolio Construction show the same methods at the level of a single deal and a whole book of holdings. Reading the Market's Language and Alternative Data cover the inputs, one from text and one from satellites, card swipes and web traffic. Agent Workflows in Finance describes how these pieces get chained into automated processes, and Crypto Markets and Decentralised Finance tests them in a market that never closes. Governance and Fiduciary Risk sits over all of it, because every page above raises the same question of who is accountable when a model is wrong.
